"Did anyone else know of your employment by Mulhall?" Mr. Garrett asked.


"Representative McDermott did," said McMichael. "I told him of having persuaded Mulhall to help him in his duties and he said to me, 'Well, Mac, I guess he's a pretty good skate,' and said, 'Yes, he is a good, square guy and he met Mulhall.'"


At the instance of McDermott, McMichael said he turned over to Mulhall the key to the room in the basement of the capitol.


"We used the room for conferences and for sleeping off drunks," the witness said. "I was drunk there."


"Did Mr. McDermott have any share in this $50 a month salary?" asked Mr. Garrett.


"Not directly as a salary from the National Association of Manufacturers," said McMichael, "but I would meet McDermott and he would say: 'Have you seen the colonel today?' I would say, 'Yes.' 'Did you get any dough?' 'Yes.' 'How much?' 'Fifty bucks.' Then he would say, 'Well, slip me ten or fifteen or twenty,' and he'd always get it."


"McDermott was generally hard up and would not give his monthly check in advance. I would take this check to a pawn broker, who would give me the cash for it and hold it until the first of the month, when it was dated. Sometimes he would give me $50 or $60."


The witness detailed his reasons for introducing McDermott to Mulhall. He said Mulhall told him that he intended to have McDermott "trimmed" and asked him to help writing letters. McMichael indignantly refused, as McDermott was his friend and employer. He then introduced the lobbyist to the congressman. After a conference, he added, Mulhall not only gave up his plan of "trimming" but also went to manufacturers in Chicago to prove his defeat. McMichael said he was positive McDermott would have been defeated in the 1910 primary but for his interposition.


McMichael also said that McDermott received letters from his brother-in-law in Chicago under his official congressional frank. During the recess of congress, he declared he was in absolute charge of Mr. McDermott.

The two months of the special session of Congress have developed a situation the like of which is not recalled by political observers in Washington. For the first time in the memory of old observers of Washington doings, the Administration is without a recognized spokesman in either house of Congress. of the International Harvester Company—the so-called harvester trust which the Federal government is seeking to dissolve under the Sherman law, lies in its monopolistic position, its superior command of capital, in guiding its connections with J. P. Morgan & Co. and John D. Rockefeller and certain objectionable competitive methods, according to Luther Conant, Jr., Commissioner of Corporations, in his report on the operations of the giant corporation, submitted to President Taft to-day.

The chief features of the International Harvester Company's operations, says Mr. Conant, are the substantial maintenance of its monopolistic position in the harvesting-machine business, originally acquired through combination, and its extensions on a large scale into new lines of the farm machinery industry. The company has been able to do this in part through the acquisition of some of its chief rivals in the harvesting machine business; in part by using its monopolistic advantage in these harvesting-machine lines to force the sale of its new lines; in part by certain objectionable competitive methods, and especially through its exceptional command of capital, itself the result of combination.

The harvester investigation was made in response to senate resolution passed several years ago. A request was made by representatives of the company that the report be withheld pending the outcome of the antitrust suit, but President Taft decided to make it public.

Not Mere Sale.

The combination, the report declares, was not, "as frequently asserted, mere sale of their properties to new interests. On this point, Mr. Conant says:

"It has been represented in formal testimony by officers of the company and its financial promoter, G. W. Perkins, then of the firm of J. P. Morgan & Co., that its organization was not the result of concerted action by the former competing owners, but merely the purchase of their properties by new and outside interests. Documentary evidence gathered by the bureau completely disposes of this contention and shows that the principal competing interests considered and discussed among themselves the formation of this combination and were active in bringing it about."

Great resources came to the company, it is asserted, through the combination, the financial support of J. P. Morgan & Co. its fiscal agents, and large loans secured from John D. Rockefeller, father-in-law of a member of the McCormick family which owns a large portion of the total stock of the corporation.

These exceptional resources, Mr. Conant maintains, not only enable the harvester company to secure the economies of large scale operations, which, as rule, give it marked advantage in manufacturing costs, but also enable it to maintain a very elaborate selling organization by virtue of the variety and extent of its business. Furthermore, they give it great advantage in extending credits to purchasers, an exceedingly important feature of the farm machinery industry."

Gets Control Secretly.

Between 1903 and 1904 the company is declared by the commissioner to have acquired secretly, control of D. M. Osborne & Co. its chief competitor; the Minnie Harvester Company, the Aultman-Miller Company and the Keystone Company. These are referred to as "bogus independents." The secret control of the Osborne Company, the report says, was maintained and concealed in some cases merely to have it advertised as an independent concern. These representations, it is alleged, were supported by its managers in sworn statements that it was an independent company. Two of the chief stockholders of the Osborne Company, Mr. Conant adds, agreed to refrain from engaging independently in the same lines of business for ten years. The report says that the concealment is not regarded by the Bureau of Corporations as justification of the practice.

These acquisitions, the report continues, were followed by the company extending its manufacture from such harvesting machinery as grain binders and mowers to the called new lines of farming tools, such as tillage implements, manure spreaders, farm wagons, gasolene engines, tractors and cream separators. Compulsion of dealers to take the company's new lines by reason of its monopolistic control of harvesting machines, says the commissioner, has been attempted with more or less success by the company's representatives.

Proved by Its Records.

Competitive methods employed by the Harvester Company, Mr. Conant, declares, have been the subject of much complaint. Regarding the charge that the company has made an effort to secure an undue proportion of local dealers in farm machinery by allotting, as rule only single brand to any one dealer in the same place, thus tending to restrict the outlet for competitors' goods, Commissioner Conant says:

"The company's own records show that this was one purpose at least in making this distribution of its brands and it appears to have had some practical effect in handicapping competition."

ing number Of settlers coming in to
occupy the agricultural districts of
the three prairie provinces. There
were those connected with the work
or securing settlers for western Cam
ada who last spring prophesied that
there would be as many as $4,000
new settlers from the United States
to Canada during the present year.
and there were those who doubted
that the previous years figures OF
$4,000 could be increased Recent
computation made by the officials OF
the immigration branch at Ottawa
show that the largest estimates made
by officials will be beaten and that
the 100000 mark from the United
States will be reached. AS great an
increase will be shown in the figures
of those who will reach Canada from
other countries this year The re-

immigration will give upward of
total of 100000 souls.


But this is not to be wondered at
when it is realized what is offering in
the three prairie provinces and also
In the coast province OF British Co
lumbia, which is also bidding strong
ly and successfully, too. for certain
class of settler. the settler who
wishes to go into mixed farming or
fruit raising. When the central por-

the railway now being constructed
there will be large areas of splendid
land available for the settler

friends say of it. James A. Flaherty,

lumbus, was in western Canada a
short time ago. He says:


''If I were a young man I would
sell out my interests in less than two
months and come right to the Cana
dian Northwest, where so many OPP
portunities abound" -Advertisement.

At the Methodist church Saturday evening, March first, at 7:30 o'clock, W. F. Nolan and Miss Erin Blacksher were married before large concourse of friends.

The holy edifice was decorated in white roses, ferns and pot flowers. Hundreds of people were in and outside of the church to witness the ceremonies which made Miss Erin Blacksher, one of St. Landry's own products and most charming and fascinating young maiden of this city, the wife of W. F. Nolan, one of Opelousas' newcomers and a very popular man both in business and the social world.

Mr. Nolan and his best man, Hugh Blacksher, brother to the bride, awaited at the altar the coming of the bride. To the strains of Mendelssohn's wedding march—rendered by Mrs. Albert Dejean on the piano, Louis White on the flute, and Chas. Sandoz on the violin—the bridal party entered the portals of the beautiful church, led by one of the bridesmaids, Miss Laura Swayze, a stately blonde of Natchez, Miss, with ease and grace. She wore a cerise satin, with an over-dress of shadow lace, trimmed in pink moss buds and foliage, and carried a bouquet of pink carnations, tied with white satin ribbon.

Next came Miss Nellie Milburn, an attractive brunette, of Gold Dust, La. She wore a Dresden chiffon, embroidered in pink, over pink messaline. She also carried a bouquet of pink carnations, with white satin bow.

Then came the maid of honor, Miss Lizzie Blacksher, the charming sister of the pretty bride. She was robed in light blue brocaded satin with an over-dress of white chiffon, trimmed in pearls, blue rosebuds and foliage. She carried a bouquet of white carnations, tied with a blue satin ribbon.

Last came the bride, leaning on the arm of her father, P. F. Blacksher, a prosperous merchant of this city. She was gowned in a white crepe de Chine, trimmed in pearls and rhinestones, over white charmeuse satin, and carried a bouquet of bridal roses, asparagus and maidenhair ferns, tied with a white satin ribbon. Over all fell the veil of illusion, fastened to the hair by orange blossoms.

During the ceremony Lange's flower song was played immediately after the knots were tied, the immediate friends and relatives of the married couple repaired to the home of the bride's parents, where they were rendered a grand reception. The house was exquisitely decorated with pot plants and ferns, and garlands of pink roses festooned the wall.

Mr. and Mrs. Blacksher and son, Joe Blacksher, welcomed the guests at the hall door. Mrs. Blacksher wore black brocaded silk, with lace over-dress, trimmed in jet. Beside these, the bridal party ably assisted in receiving. Mrs. Lorenzo Mornhinveg ushered the guests into the dining-room, where the center table was beautifully decorated for the occasion. From the ceiling, attached to lights above, four streamers of pink tulle fell to the four corners of the table. Here Mesdames Jos. Lawler, T. H. Harris, of Baton Rouge, and O. A. Durio, assisted by the following little girls, dressed in white with pink sashes: Lena Loeb, Myrtle Mornhinveg, Mamie Lawler and Willemette Durio, served cakes and cream.

From the dining-room the guests were ushered into the hall, where they were served to punch, by Mrs. Remit Mornhinveg.

The married couple left for Lafayette in William T. Stewart's car, accompanied by Mr. and Mrs. Stewart, where they went to board a Southern Pacific train for New Orleans, from whence they went to Washington for the Inauguration, thence New York, Niagara Falls and other eastern points.

Mr. and Mrs. Nolan were the recipients of many beautiful and appropriate presents. To them the Clarion wishes most happy and long-lived married life.—St. Landry Clarion.

Majors, who gave grand address, reviewing the achievements in road building within the last few months, and emphasizing the necessity of able, energetic, and persistent efforts for the construction of good roads. Sadds for Oklahoma and Mr. Batzjer of Rogers for Arkansas, which latter response deserving especial mention as he certainly did full credit to himself and Northwest Arkansas. PHOENIX, Jan. 24—P. Joseph Carney and associates have taken bond and option on the famous old Bulldog mine and thirteen surrounding claims. Within thirty days they will have a large force at work doing active development work. Their intention is to spend a large sum in solving the fault system and determining just exactly what the property is worth.

The fourteen claims taken over are half a mile north of George L. Young's Mammoth mine sixteen miles northeast of Mesa. The Bulldog is one of the old producers of the Goldfield district. Mr. Carney estimates that $685,000 has been taken from surface workings on the Bulldog claim.

A number of persons held the claims and much time was spent in closing the deal. It is now completed, however, and nothing is in the way of an active campaign of development. The bondholders have ample capital.

The main ledge of the group is the Bulldog, which has an average width of 15 feet. It is porphyry, heavily shot with manganese, and lies between granite walls. Several cross veins intersect it. These veins are one to two feet wide. All have the appearance of being true fault assures, and it is believed that great ore bodies lie below. Much work will be required, however, to solve the fault system.

On the surface the Bulldog vein averages $40 a ton in gold, while the cross assures run from $30 to $40. Values increase steadily with depth wherever any work has been done.

The deepest shaft is down 112 feet on the Bulldog vein. From this level 500 feet of drifts have been run. Samples were taken across five-foot face in one of the drifts and they gave returns of $500.

Altogether the former owners of the group did about one thousand feet of development work. They were constantly baffled by the faulty system, there being much faulting throughout that entire region. Mr. Carney is confident that the ore is there and that only little persistence is required to find it.

"In my opinion the Bulldog will be proved to be a great gold dissemination, the same as the Ray is a copper dissemination," he said this morning. An important problem at the Bulldog is that of water. If the bondholders decide to exercise their option they will lay a pipe from the Salt river, eight miles north, and pump water to the property for a reduction plant and camp purposes.

The electric transmission line from Roosevelt runs close to the Bulldog. This line will be tapped and electricity used for power in the development work.

There is a ten horsepower gasoline engine, a pump and other machinery at the Bulldog. Additional machinery will be installed as soon as possible.

London, July 16.—The most astonishing and present the most mysterious jewel robbery of the present century is associated with the disappearance of a pearl necklace valued at $4,000 during transit from Paris to London. The necklace was mailed in Paris on Tuesday evening and was addressed to Mayer, a diamond merchant, No. 15 Hatton Garden, London. It was contained in a package measuring 10 1/2 inches. The package was registered and insured at Lloyds for an enormous sum. In this there was nothing unusual. It is the custom to send jewelry of great value from Paris to London, and vice versa, through the registered mail, because that means of transit is considered safer than intrusting such valuables to special messengers.

In due course a package of the size and weight that was expected, and bearing the seals of Mayer's Paris agent, was delivered yesterday morning at Mayer's place of business in Hatton Garden, but with the opening of the case came terrible shock for Mayer, for in place of the superb necklace that the case had contained, nothing more was found than a few pieces of sugar shaped into thin cubes and obviously of French manufacture. This fact makes it evident that the substitution must have taken place somewhere on the other side of the channel.

Without delay the police were communicated with, and at the same time the Paris agent was summoned both by telephone and by telegraph. On receipt of the news, the Paris agent started for London forthwith. He was met at Charing Cross by Mayer and Chief Inspector Ward of Scotland Yard. CLEVELAND, Ohio, Nov. 13.—Never
in the history of navigation on the
Great Lakes has a storm claimed such
toll of human life and damage to
shipping as the terrific blizzard which
swept over four of the big fresh water
bodies the early part of this week.
Latest reports today place the num-
ber of missing sailors on shipwrecked
vessels at 150.

There is a growing fear today that
four steel steamers on Lake Huron,
carrying crews of twenty men each
have been lost. The vessels are over
highly hours overdue and still unreported.

A score of bodies have already been
recovered on Lakes Huron and Super-
ior, washed up with the wreckage
of numerous boats.

A majority of the vessels reported
lost or missing were owned by companies or individuals and ex-
perts here today agreed that the total
loss will probably reach $3,200,000.
That amount is based on latest re-
ports received and includes the mis-
sing vessels. However, it does not in-
clude loss of cargoes, which will eas-
ily run into $1,000,600.

The total number of big vessels
lost will reach twenty-five, it was es-
timated today.

Lake Huron claimed the biggest toll
of human life. Its west shore, usually
a weather shore, harbored many ves-
sels when the storm broke. The wind
shifted trickily, however, and the
east shore received the full force of
the seventy mile gale, driving before
it a mass of blinding sleet and snow.
Huge seas swept over the vessels,
taking with them not only cabins and
upper works but also human beings,
the sailors having become the great
lake's biggest graveyard.

Preparedness went for naught in
this storm. The staunchest vessels,
representing the best in marine archi-
tecture of the United States, Canada,
New England and Scotland were pounded
to pieces by the gale. All were help-
less before the mad fury of the storm.

The modern steel steamer H. M.
Dannas could not have been in better
shape. She was piled on the beach at
Point Aux Barques and broke in two.
The James Carruthers, the largest
steamer ever turned out of a Cana-
dian shipyard, is now reported lost
in Lake Huron.

Near to Lake Huron, Lake Superior
claimed the biggest toll of life and
property. The storm on Lake Super-
ior was as severe as that on Lake
Huron, but the wind did not shift,
blowing steadily from the northwest.
There can be no estimate made at
this time of loss to small vessels and
lives along the lakes. All along both
the west and east shores of the lower
peninsula of Michigan, small craft
were smashed and sunk by the storm.
Docks and piers were washed away at
various ports and even breakwaters
were torn apart.

Chicago suffered heavy loss to its
marine shipping and many boulevards
were washed out.

Sioux CITY. Aug. 15.—While a three
months old baby girl lay on a bench
in the Great Northern railroad station
yesterday kicking and cooing in great
glee, her mother is supposed to have

Shortly after the Great Northern

the station yesterday morning at 3.50,
a Frenchman and his wife approached
the ticket agent at the station and in-
quired where the parents of the child
in the women's waiting room were, as
there was one there and no one seemed
to be around to take care of it.


R. A. Rasmussen, ticket agent, in-

baby lying on one of the benches,
wrapped in a blanket. She was not the
least bit excited or afraid, but lay coo-
ing and laughing and kicking her feet
in the air. Attached to the little one's
dress was a note which read:


This baby was born May 11, 1913.
To finder please care for this baby.
"School Girl"

and Mrs. Anna Louisa Seaman

has been placed in the Florence Crit-
ten home.

dent that until the time of its aban-
donment the child had had the best of
attention.

scrawl, as if prepared in great haste

with the purpose of abandoning the
baby and taking the train for the
north. Others are inclined to think
that the leaving of the child in the
station, so near train time, was mere
blindness and the mother is still in the
city.

adoption at the home.

great variety of physiological causes
and improper soil conditions. During
the past year, the writer has had the

observed carefully the varied condi

been found growing The disease has
been found on trees growing on all
sorts of soils and under all sorts of
cultural conditions. 1t has been found
on light soils and wet soils, on deep
soils and shallow soils, on bottom
lands and hillsides, on north slopes
and south slopes, and on hilltops. The
disease exists in both irrigated and
non-irrigated sections. 1t seems to be
equally prevalent in orchards where
clean culture is practised and in or
chards where various systems of in
ter-cropping are employed. Orchards
which have been allowed to grow up
to weeds are no more badly infected
than orchards well cared for. 1t would
seem, therefore. that neither soil con-
ditions nor cultural practices bear any
direct Relationship to the cause of the
disease.

to be infectious and will spread from
tree to tree. Until something more
definite can be learned regarding the
specific cause of the disease infected
branches should be cut out at once and
burned Fortunately, the disease make

and if pruning is done as soon as the
symptoms appear, it should not be diff
ficult to control

Washington, June 23—Democrats opposed to free sugar enlivened the Senate caucus late to-day in making their final effort to change the schedule before the tariff bill should reach the Senate for general debate.

Senators Shafroth, of Colorado, and Walsh, of Montana, took the floor when the schedule suddenly was reached in the late afternoon. It had not been expected that the caucus would reach sugar before tomorrow, but the wool and wood schedules were rushed through, with little discussion and before once the decks were cleared for the most determined internecine party struggle.

Senator Shafroth was the first speaker. Coming from Colorado, beet sugar being his interest, he made vigorous plea for elimination of the provision for free sugar in three years. He submitted many briefs and statistics to support the contention of the beet sugar manufacturers that free sugar would mean the gripping, if not the death, of the industry.

Senator Walsh, of Montana, who also will make a fight against free wool, is standing by the anti-free sugar Senators in the caucus fight. He followed Senator Shafroth and had not closed when the caucus adjourned until tomorrow.

Until sugar was reached, the caucus had been harmonious. No change was made in the report of the majority members of the Finance Committee on the wool and wooden manufactures schedule. The only material change in this from the Underwood bill was the free listing of cedar boards and other cabinet woods.

In the metal schedule there were four votes taken on committee amendments, and in each case the committee was sustained. Aluminium in the crude state was left at cents a pound and in sheets and plates at 3 1/2 cents a pound.

The committee's increase from 1 to 1/2 of cent a pound on lead ore was also sustained, as were its amendments increasing the duty on zinc ore from 10 to 12 1/2 per cent advance ad valorem and zinc in pigs from 10 to 15 per cent. An effort to put hand saws and other common tools on the free list was not successful, and a few small items in the schedule were referred for later determination.

took place Saturday afternoon at the
Loughead ranch, three miles
west of the mountain town of La
Veta, when an automobile containing
four guards, the driver and one miner
was ambushed by a gang of men and
three of them killed and two wounded.
The Dead—Harry Bryan, 1882 Ogden
street, Denver, captain of guards;
Walter Whitten, Carlton hotel, Den-
ver, guard; Luke Terry, Colorado
Springs, chauffeur.


The Wounded—R. G. Adams, Arri-
ba, Colo., shot through left arm and
right foot; William Gamblin, miner,
shot through right lung.


The place where the shooting took
place is ideal for an ambush. The road
winds out of La Veta and runs along
and up hill. At the right of the hill,
where the road starts up, the
Loughead reservoir held in by a dirt
embankment. It was from this en-
bankment that the strikers did their
firing.


The riddled automobile stood Sat-
urday night in the same spot where
the stiffening hands of the chauffeur
had stopped it, Terry slipped down
in his seat still holding the wheel.


Fifty yards back Captain Bryan lay
face downward with his gun under
him. Whitten, twenty yards back of
the machine, lay on his back. The
machine was riddled with bullets.
Gamblin is at the Owen ranch. He is
not in dangerous condition. R. G.
Adams was taken to the office of Dr.
Lamm.


General Chase Says Situation Critical.


Trinidad.—Adjutant General John
Chase regards the situation in the
strike zones of southern Colorado as
most serious, following a day of
bloodshed and violence. The streets
of Trinidad and every section of the
strike district are being guarded by
militiamen to prevent further out-
breaks.


One non-union miner shot and
killed and one striker wounded at Ag-
uilar; mine clerk assaulted, beaten
and left for dead by strikers at the
McLaughlin mine three miles south of
Trinidad; two miners beaten by strik-
ers at Starkville; camp marshal
captured by strikers, disarmed and
driven from Segundo, and skirmish
between strikers and military guards
at Forbes. It is the record of twenty-four
hours in the Las Animas county dis-
trict since General Chase left Denver
for his military headquarters here.


Five bridges of the Denver & Rio
Grande main line between Cucharas
and Rouse Junction have been
burned.


Strikebreaker Slain Near Aguilar.


Pedro Armijo, a non-union miner
from the Ravenwood mine in Huer-
fano county, was shot and killed on
the outskirts of Aguilar by one of a
group of six strikers from the Aguilar
tent colony who, it is reported, had
followed and surrounded him on his
way to Lynn station to take train
for Walsenburg.


Terror Rules Coal District.


Walsenburg, Colo., Nov. 10.—With
R. G. Adams, the fourth of the men
shot in the ambuscade near La Veta
Saturday afternoon, dead in the hos-
pital at Pueblo, the feeling of horror
in this district over the killing has
intensified.


That the reign of terror is on again
is freely expressed by citizens. The
strained feeling that pervaded both
La Veta and Aguilar during Saturday
and ended in killings, was felt at
Walsenburg up until late hour Sun-
day night. It broke once when strik-
ers caught Neal McDerhott, fire-boss
from the Maitland mine, before the
Star theatre and beat him.

As the express elevator shot upward, he passed a long slender hand across his eyes. The rapid motion confused him still. The car stopped, and the metallic gates chanced open. Darrow obediently stepped forth. Only when the elevator had disappeared did his upward glance bring to him the knowledge that he had disembarked one floor too soon.


Darrow's eye fell on a lettered sign outside the nearest door. He smiled a slow red-lipped smile beneath his small silky mustache, dropped his black eyelashes in flicker of reminiscence, hesitated a moment, then stepped languidly forward and opened the door. The sign indicated the headquarters of the very modest commissionership behind which McCarthy chose to work. McCarthy, quite simply, at that time owned New York.


As Darrow entered, McCarthy hung up the telephone receiver with a smash, and sat gazing at the instrument. After a moment he turned his small bright eyes toward the new corner.


"Hello, Perc," he growled. "Didn't see you. Say, I'm so mad my skin cracks. Just now some measly little shrimp called me up from a public booth. What ye suppose he wanted, now? Oh, nothin'! Just told me in so many words for me to pack up my little trunk and sail for Europe and never come back. That's all! He give me until Sunday, too!" McCarthy barked out a short laugh, and reached for a cigarbox, which he held out to Darrow.

ingly, have fixed standard of tips

size of their tips is a sort of compro-
mise between obedience to custom
and their practice of paying for all
service what it is worth.

railway or hotel employe is not
moved by any sentiment of charity.

terness that he is paying to the em-
ploye wages which his employer ought
to pay him.

posed employer for the privilege of

prey upon the public, and as the
ex-tip recipient states, the choicest
victims are found among the vulgar
who often cannot afford the tips they
bestow.

WASHINGTON, Mar. 27.—An impressive exhibit of the mineral resources of the sixteen southern states whose industries are included in the exhibit of the Southern Commercial Congress is seen in a large wall map which has just been specially compiled by the United States Geological Survey for the use of the congress. The minerals of the several areas are shown on the map in appropriate colors and tints, some of which are of course superimposed on others.

Coal is the premier mineral resource of the southern states. The map shows large areas of workable bituminous coal in Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, Oklahoma and Texas, and smaller areas in Georgia and North Carolina. The Geological Survey's estimate of the original tonnage (in the ground) of the southern coal fields is 615,557,100,000 short tons; the total production to January 1, 1912, was 1,224,552,255 tons. The area of the southern coal fields containing workable coal is shown as 104,000 square miles and that which may contain workable coal as 146,700 square miles additional.

The area distribution of oil and natural gas as shown on the map is very inconspicuous compared with the great coal areas. The value of the oil and natural gas produced in 1911 was, however, nearly three-fourths that of the coal produced in the same year. The value of the coal produced in 1911 was $24,000,000,900; that of oil and gas was $85,100,000.

Clay products of the southern states in 1911 amounted to more than $780,100,000 and the Geological Survey is authority for the statement that the southern deposits probably exceed in area and volume those of any other portion of the United States of the same size.

The lead and zinc produced in the southern states in 1911 was valued at $16,514,560. The stone was valued at $14,275,155 and is shown on the map to be well distributed. The production of phosphate is essentially southern industry and the value of the output of 1911 was $11,560,511.

Of iron ore deposits, large areas are indicated on the map in Missouri, Arkansas, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia, and North Carolina and smaller bodies in Maryland, Alabama, Texas, South Carolina, and Georgia. The output from the ten producing southern states in 1911 was valued at $7,379,257. An estimate of the available iron ore reserves in the Southern states by C. Willard Hayes, formerly chief geologist of the United States Geological Survey, places it at 500,000,000 long tons, together with a much larger quantity of low grade ore. Copper is produced in seven of the Southern states; the value of the 1911 output was $2,455,565.

This large map shows twenty-five mineral deposits of the Southern states, the annual output of which is valued at $100,000 or less.

San Francisco, Cal, July 8, 1913.


To All Central Labor Councils, Greetings:


Dear Sirs and Brothers—The Light and Power Council of California desires to submit the following on behalf of the men out on strike against the Pacific Gas and Electric company for the consideration of organized labor in the United States and Canada and trusts that your organization will see fit to take favorable action in this matter and support the strikers morally and financially to the fullest extent of your resources.


For years the workers of the Light and Power industry have had powerful corporations to contend with for living wages and conditions. In many instances these corporations consist solely in fighting the organization of their employees and maintain departments for this purpose, as in the case of the corporations in Los Angeles. In and around the Bay Cities some individual organizations have been more or less successful in getting somewhere near equitable wages through their unions, but year after year this has been made harder and harder.


Recognizing this fact and that something had to be done in the matter, the Light and Power Council of California was organized February 10, 1913, and is at present composed of the following crafts:


Boiler Makers, Stationary Firemen, Machinists, Gas Workers, Electrical Workers.


In the case of the latter a condition exists on the coast for which neither the Electrical Workers nor any other element in organized labor in the West is responsible, namely, the non-affiliation of the organized Light and Power Electrical Workers with the American Federation of Labor, but these men are all true trade unionists, progressive and true blue, hence in the formation of the Light and Power Council, we found that if we were to be successful we would have to take conditions as they presented themselves from which we were to obtain results. Three years ago the machinists asked the gas company for an eight-hour day and were refused. A strike ensued and the machinists were whipped by the company. The gas workers have been contending for better wages and conditions, and last year the company refused any increase to their men as well as to the electrical workers, and even refused to arbitrate the matter. The firemen for years have been contending for a six-day week, but have been unable to gain same through their individual organization.


After the formation of the Light and Power Council, joint agreements were drawn up and presented through same to the gas company, who first refused recognition of the Council, stating that they would only do business with individual organizations. A vote was taken on the matter from our affiliated locals and as a result of this vote the company changed their attitude and agreed to recognize our council.  Nature is so prodigal with her flor al gifts. and flowers are in such gen. eral use everywhere at all times, 1t would at first seem as if nothing new could be said on this subject Flow CTS fill the cradle, we are married un- der floral bell. our coffin Is covered with Fragrant offerings, and, as we lie at peace, every spring the sod above us is bright with buttercups and the snowy daisies. Could we imagine Easter day or May day without blossoms, or Decoration day with no wreaths of flowers? But just because flowers run into such infinite varieties, and their phases are so inexhaustible. I may hit upon something fresh to some of my hearers.

 Did it ever occur to you at Society function where blue. red. or pink, is the Sought-after color scheme, that mother nature, is the greatest color scheme artist. and that our best effects are feeble limitations of her lavish dis plays. have never been to Japan in cherry blossom time, but more than once been through the Hall peach or chardS in Georgia and South Carolina, and through their Northern rivals at Glastonbury, when there were miles up-

 

 of you no doubt. on your way to Washington in late July. have seen the pink clouds of marShmallow resting on the Jersey marshes. Under this smiling mask does Nature hide her seething clouds of deadly mosquitoes.

 l know small meadow almost with in cannon-shot of this hall where the changing color scheme is really won deTful. A solid mass of marsh-ma goldS in April is followed in May by a pink blanket of Painted Cup,-not dabs of tint but great half-acre splashes of color. This shifts in June to buttercups. veritable cloth of gold, followed at once by a reflection of heavens own hue from great beds of Iris, slowly fringed with ox-eyed, white, and yellow daisies, later picked out with royal cardinal, and as fin ishing master touch with the perfect cerulean or fringed gentian. It Is a garden, by the side of which our color schemes are but fade-aways. Four sorts of orchids are found in this meadow = purple e-fringed, maiden's tresses, pogonies. and calopogons- which we call "callies'' and "pogies" oftener. Reckoning the more modest flowers and all the tiny towering grasses on this one meadow, they must run into a century of different blossom ing plants.

 Another of Natures changing color schemes Is effectively shown to travel CTS up and down over Thames river between New London and Norwich. Shad- blows in early May first attract the attention like white nile-stones, followed in greater profusion by dog wood, and then in June the showy mountain laurel on both sides of the river charms all ages. relieved on the sand banks and railroad cuts by solid rods of June pinks. These pinks, com- mon in the Cowen part of the country, I do not find here-the nearest I have observed them is at Wauregan. The highest up the Thames River l ever found marshmallow was at the brack- ish outlet of Poquetannoc Cove. The Clintonia, quite common in the Eng fish Neighborhood, do not find as far south as Norwich.

 Still another novel color-scheme I saw near Avalon at Santa Catalina Island in the Pacific Ocean where we look through glaSS-bottomed boats down at tall marine growths of every shade of color, through which clear red fish were slowly moving like the most brilliant of waving flowers.

 I recall at Del Coronado, Coronado Beach, California, my ecstacy at first seeing a great Bourgainville in full flower, like a glorified purple wistaria. And my delight to see the rubber tree jungle below Palm Beach, Florida lit up with showy scarlet hibiscus. But right here nearer home. in Norwich, l know a white wistaria. so large that when bushels of the white raceineS were taken to cover a cemetery lot. the loss could not be noticed.

 We are improving steadily in our home decorations. In my childhood there was not crimson rambler or Japan snowball in Connecticut. Now

 T . sc without them. And now, thanks to the department stores with their spring sales of German rosebushes, every boy and girl knows the General Jack the Dorothy Perkins. the Marshall Mel Magma Charta, and the Paul Neron. But with the coming of new favorites, we are missing some of the old friends like the hollyhock. I knew a skillful florist who produced good effects in corners and borders by blossOming Of some of our homeliest garden-veg- etables like rhubarb. horse radish, cress, and artickokes. This same ec- centric florist raised peach trees, quince bushes, and Crab trees, just for tbas. blossoms. But really, is their any thing sweeter than Crabapple? show fer than a spray bouquet of peach bloom and can orange or magnolia, leaves and all. stand beside the deli- cate, refined shading on quince blos- soms.

 Many journeys big and litufe have I taken after rare and favorite wild flowers in their haunts. It is a com- mon mistake to suppose that arbutus grows only in New England: I have seen it in abundance at Camden, South Carolina, and between Southern Pines and Pinehurst, North Carolina. While after arbutus near CarneFS Hump, in the Green mountains I saw my first, last and only wild black bear; and while vainly seeking the red Cape Cod water lily, I met my first wild deer. From Mt. Misery Voluntown, one holiday, I brought to town 40 lbs. of brook trout and a bushel of arbutus. From the Tucker district Killingly. as late as May 2, 1 got two trout-creelS full of the real .pinky- pink arbntus, and two quarts of checkerberries. Never suck the petals of trailing arbutus, for it is a ground laurel. and all laurels are more or less poisonous. On my table blossoms, mighty pretty to look at but deadly in it's effect on stock. if eaten freely.

 For many years on June 1. I drove to a, pasture on Blue Hill, Bozrah, half a mile from any house. after double jonquils: and repeatedly, on June 10th to a small hidden meadow near Salem, after Calopogons, at one time pro- curing enough to give bunch to ev- cry bank of Norwich. "Callies" lack the fragrance of pogonias which come earlier. But for doubly distilled di- vine essence of all sweets, commend me, to the smaller yellow ladies slip per. Nature is so prodigal with her floral gifts, and flowers are in such general use everywhere at all times, it would at first seem as if nothing new could be said on this subject. Flowers fill the cradle, we are married under floral bells, our coffin is covered with fragrant offerings, and, as we lie at peace, every spring the sod above us is bright with buttercups and the snowy daisies. Could we imagine Easter day or May day without blossoms, or Decoration day with no wreaths of flowers? But just because flowers run into such infinite varieties, and their phases are so inexhaustible, I may hit upon something fresh to some of my hearers.

Did it ever occur to you at Society function where blue, red, or pink, is the sought-after color scheme, that mother nature, is the greatest color scheme artist, and that our best effects are feeble limitations of her lavish displays. I have never been to Japan in cherry blossom time, but more than once been through the peach or orchards in Georgia and South Carolina, and through their Northern rivals at Glastonbury, when there were miles up—

You, no doubt, on your way to Washington in late July, have seen the pink clouds of marshmallow resting on the Jersey marshes. Under this smiling mask does Nature hide her seething clouds of deadly mosquitoes.

I know a small meadow almost within cannon-shot of this hall where the changing color scheme is really wonderful. A solid mass of marsh-mallow gold in April is followed in May by a pink blanket of Painted Cup—not dabs of tint but great half-acre splashes of color. This shifts in June to buttercups, veritable cloth of gold, followed at once by a reflection of heaven's own hue from great beds of Iris, slowly fringed with ox-eyed, white, and yellow daisies, later picked out with royal cardinal, and as finishing master touch with the perfect cerulean or fringed gentian. It is a garden, by the side of which our color schemes are but fade-aways. Four sorts of orchids are found in this meadow—purple e-fringed, maiden's tresses, pogonias, and calopogons—which we call "callies" and "pogies" oftener. Reckoning the more modest flowers and all the tiny towering grasses on this one meadow, they must run into a century of different blossoming plants.

Another of Nature's changing color schemes is effectively shown to travel up and down over Thames river between New London and Norwich. Shadblows in early May first attract the attention like white Nile-stones, followed in greater profusion by dogwood, and then in June the showy mountain laurel on both sides of the river charms all ages, relieved on the sand banks and railroad cuts by solid rods of June pinks. These pinks, common in the Cowen part of the country, I do not find here—the nearest I have observed them is at Wauregan. The highest up the Thames River I ever found marshmallow was at the brackish outlet of Poquetannoc Cove. The Clintonia, quite common in the English neighborhood, I do not find as far south as Norwich.

Still another novel color-scheme I saw near Avalon at Santa Catalina Island in the Pacific Ocean where we look through glass-bottomed boats down at tall marine growths of every shade of color, through which clear red fish were slowly moving like the most brilliant of waving flowers.

I recall at Del Coronado, Coronado Beach, California, my ecstasy at first seeing a great Bougainvillea in full flower, like a glorified purple wistaria. And my delight to see the rubber tree jungle below Palm Beach, Florida lit up with showy scarlet hibiscus. But right here nearer home, in Norwich, I know a white wistaria, so large that when bushels of the white racemes were taken to cover a cemetery lot, the loss could not be noticed.

We are improving steadily in our home decorations. In my childhood there was not crimson rambler or Japan snowball in Connecticut. Now we can't see without them. And now, thanks to the department stores with their spring sales of German rosebushes, every boy and girl knows the General Jack, the Dorothy Perkins, the Marshall Mel, Magma Charta, and the Paul Neron. But with the coming of new favorites, we are missing some of the old friends like the hollyhock. I knew a skillful florist who produced good effects in corners and borders by blossoming of some of our homeliest garden-vegetables like rhubarb, horseradish, cress, and artichokes. This same eccentric florist raised peach trees, quince bushes, and crab trees, just for their blossoms. But really, is there anything sweeter than crabapple? Or fairer than a spray bouquet of peach bloom and canna orange or magnolia, leaves and all, stand beside the delicate, refined shading on quince blossoms.

Many journeys big and little have I taken after rare and favorite wild flowers in their haunts. It is a common mistake to suppose that arbutus grows only in New England; I have seen it in abundance at Camden, South Carolina, and between Southern Pines and Pinehurst, North Carolina. Misery Voluntown, one holiday, I brought to town 40 lbs. of brook trout and a bushel of arbutus. and squirrels are her friends and keep
her company. Most of the time she
carries the mail on horseback. At
times, in good weather, however, when
the roads are worn down hard and
smooth, she uses a single buggy. Be-
sides Henderson and Bakersfield, she
serves two other towns en route:
Gamaliel and Custer, both roadside
villages, but with large post office pat-
ronage. The most dreaded part of her
trip at times is crossing the North
Fork river, a mountain stream nearly
as large as the White river, which at
times gets to be a raging mountain
torrent. The stream is fordable at low
water, but when it goes on a rampage
it is dangerous even for ferryboats
to cross. One time when it was past
fording she swam her horse across in
order to get her mail to its destination
that night. She came out on the op-
posite bank with dripping skirts, but
with mail high and dry on her shoul-
ders.

In the spring and summer the route
is pleasant to ride, as some of the
finest scenery in the Ozarks lies along
the way. Wild flowers and grass cover
the woods floor and the hills are a
mass of green, with the rocks of the
river bluffs sticking out in bare splen-
dor. In autumn, too, it is beautiful,
when the woods present an ever
changing color, but when the winter
winds begin to blow and the days of
falling snow and binding, biting sleet

spirit of a man, but Floe sticks to her
post. The winter season is short and
the warm spring days to come buoy
her up.

her out. Hannah or Pearl goes after
the mail at Henderson in the morning
and brings it to the house, where Floe
picks it up and carries it on to Bakers-
field and brings back the morning mail
from that point. They take it then to
Henderson for her, letting her get off

stores for them when they are too
busy to go to town.

man. The family live on a farm and

them. Boys, he says, are always mak-
ing the old folks trouble.

the carrying of the mail so that all got
a chance at the district school, going
from there to the academy at Mountain
Home and from there into more
profitable employment or to make
happy homes of their own. Those that
are married are happily married, and
the others who are not at home are
holding lucrative business positions.

It means that as in the dawning of the natural day the darkness flees gradually, so now in the dawning of the New Dispensation, Messiah's Day, a thousand years long, the light of Divine Truth is shining more and more clearly. It is scattering our darkness and our fears, and enabling us, as people of God, more and more to love the great Fountain of blessing, from whom cometh every good and every perfect gift.


Now we see that the faults which have been found with the Bible belong not to it. It is consistent. It contains the Divine Plan, or Program, so comprehensive and so beautiful as to be heart-assuring that it is of God and not of man. No human mind could possibly devise the glorious features of God's Plan, providing a place on the Heavenly plane for the elect Church, and a place on the earthly plane for Adam and all his race—as many of them as will accept the offer, when clearly and distinctly presented to them, when the blind eyes shall be opened and all the deaf ears shall be unstopped.—Isaiah 59:5, 6.


We see, then, my dear brethren, that the death of Christ is, by God's arrangement, the most important fact in the whole world's history. The next in importance is His resurrection from the dead and ascension to glory. His work for man will be at His Second Coming: He will establish His Heaven Kingdom, and rule, bless and uplift the world to all that was lost in Adam and redeemed at Calvary—the Bride of Christ sharing with her Lord in all that great and wonderful work, being qualified thereto by her share with Him in the First Resurrection.—Revelation 20:4.

Particularly impressive and significant were a map of the district hanging over the congressman's desk and an oil painting of the Atkins mansion at Bayport which, with the iron dogs and urns conspicuous in its foreground, occupied the middle of the largest wall space.

The cheery fire was very comforting on a night like this, for the sleet was driving against the windowpanes, the sidewalks were ankle deep in slush, and the wet, cold wind from the Potomac was whistling down the street. Somewhere about the house an unfastened shutter slammed in the gusts. Mr. Atkins should have been extremely comfortable as he sat there by the fire. He had spent many comfortable winters in that room. But now there was a frown on his face as he read the letter in his hand. It was from Simpson and stated among other things, that Cyrus Whitaker had been absent from Bayport for over two weeks and that no one seemed to know where he had gone. "The idea seems to be that he started for Washington," wrote Tad, "but if that is so it is queer you haven't seen him; am suspicious that he is up to something about that harbor business. I should keep my eye peeled if I was you."

Alicia, the Atkins hopeful, rustled into the room.

Muscatine, Ia., May 7.—Several persons received injuries in the derailment of Rock Island passenger train number 404, which occurred yesterday morning on the Montezuma branch at a point about 11 miles west of Nichols.

A defective rail is believed to have caused the cars to leave the track. Two coaches were thrown down an embankment at the side of the right of way.

Charles Diffey, of Lone Tree, was injured internally, while J. R. Fisher received bruises on the cheek and hip. A woman, whose name was not learned, was badly cut about the face by flying glass.


STATE BANKERS INSPECT


AMES COLLEGE AFFAIRS


Ames, Ia., May 15.—Iowa State college and the Ames Commercial club have united in planning the reception and entertainment of at least 100 members of the Iowa State Bankers association who have abandoned their annual convention in Des Moines today for an afternoon inspecting the state college.

James Wilson, former secretary of the Department of Agriculture, now at his home near Ames taking a short rest prior to his leaving for Europe with the committee appointed to study European agriculture, could not deliver the address to the financiers.

Instead of Mr. Wilson, J. D. Wood, of Joliet, Ill., spoke on farm credits. Other arrangements made it possible for President W. G. Brown of the New York Central railway system to address the bankers as planned.


MYSTERY IN DEATH OF


VETERAN AT ATLANTIC


Atlantic, Ia., May 25.—The coroner's jury, which investigated the death of Noah Guessford, 75 years old, civil war veteran, who died mysteriously in his home here, found that he came to his death from poison administered in a manner as to us unknown.

Clyde Guessford, of Eldon, was called here and does not believe that anyone contributed to his father's death. His parents had been divorced and it is the son's belief that his father became disheartened by illness and took the poison either by mistake or otherwise.

Prevention of waste of our natural

echoes it as a slogan of conservation.
Waste is so intimate, in the associa-

Sin that it has no champion. In econ

despicable place.


In the problems which the Conserva-
tion Congress in session has before it
now prevention of waste is tremen-
deus item. 1t is easy to observe that
Some of our resources have been
wasted The maximum of enjoyment
has not been gotten out of what has
been expended from the once-thought
immeasurable stores which Nature
planted in this wonderfully rich land.
Forests, lands, mines, streams, and all
the beasts of the field, fowls of the air,
and fishes of the sea, have been ex-
plotted extravagantly. The United
States is only now beginning to recover
from the wild prodigality of their
youth to recognize that they have been
wasting a splendid patrimony, and must
pause and take stock before there is
nothing left.


But this pause should not be COM
plete stop of the enjoyment of our re-
sources. Prevention of use is hardly
better than prevention of waste. A re-
source which lies idle may hold high
potentiality, yet profit no one. In its
consideration of this delicate line be-
tween wastefulness and usefulness the
Conservation Congress, whose opinions
naturally are a high power in the de-
termination of questions relating to Our
natural resources, has a difficult prob
lem.


Into that part of this problem re-
lating to water power differences be-
tween States and Federal rights have
come, perhaps more bitterly than ever
before To give over to the States the
exclusive control of forests and streams
and mineral and agricultural lands
within their respective borders would
be impossible. To take away from the
States absolutely all the control over
those resources they now exercise
would be unwise. Finding the happy
mean is the task before the Conserva-
ton Congress.


The "federalists" in the Congress
have a fine theory for conservation un-
der the direction OF the national gov
ernment, and many of their practices,
too, are proper. At the same time it
has to be recognized that there are now
in use-benefcient use-water powers
which, under the "federalistS' theory,
would not be in use They would be,
the States rights men" assert, locked
up'-reserved rather than conserved.
What is needed is that the conserva-
tionists of the two parties should agree
upon a way III which to permit a use
of these water powers without permit
ting them to pass entirely out of con-.
troll of either the Federal or State gov
ernments. Perhaps the wisest way of
conserving water powers would be to
allow no "indeterminate" or permanent
charters to the private developers of
these resources; to keep vested in the
Federal Government control of all
water power developments in inter
state streams or directly affecting the
navigability of streams; and to leave
with the States the control of intrastate
streams except where they are naviga-
bic. In these enlightened days, when
all the Dustin in the world does not
suffice to make trusts an impossibiIity
but when public sentiment and the
power it wields can make trusts good"
there surely can be found better way
to defy a water power trust than TO
lock up that resource.

Cubs were there last they stopped at
first class hotel, European plan, and
most of them ate their meals at big
beanery.


These facts are cited to show how
ball players manage to save money.
While the teams are on the road the
players have the privilege of eating at
their hotel or outside. If they elect to
satisfy the inner man away from the
hotel they are allowed to charge so a
day for meals. By spending 80 cents
for breakfast, 40 cents for lunch and
80 cents for dinner they are able to
make money in excess of their salaries.


One of the big league teams recently
rode from St. Louis to New York
on 26-hour train. Each player was
allowed to put in bill for meals on
the train not to exceed $3.50. There
were three meals, yet practically all
of the players sidestepped breakfast
and supper, having a big feed at the
noon hour. When the train reached
station with lunch room—it might
have been eepsie—several play
ers dubbed together and hurriedly
bought four sandwiches, two bananas
and bottle of milk, while the others,
arriving at the Grand Central station,
made bee line for coffee and cake
room. When Jimmy Sheckard was a
member of the Brooklyn team he made
himself ill by eating irregular meals.
He used to leap off the train while on
the road at lunch towns and buy fruit,
hard boiled eggs or sandwiches. He
devoured those things in addition to
the regular meals in the dining car be-
cause he always was hungry. But
Sheckard was an exception to the gen-
eral rule.

the interests of the great fertilize-
r concerns. Some experiments made

ally more profitable to depend upon

Castine, Me.—July 2.—(Special.—To-day's meetings of superintendents of schools at their annual conference at the place developed lively interest in all topics. Supt. F. G. Marshall of Augusta talked on the form and arrangement of school reports of large towns and cities. He showed that the modern school report of large town or city serves three distinct purposes: It enables the reporting superintendent to measure his own work. It presents to his fellow superintendents such items of interest as will enable them to gain professional knowledge of their school system. It presents to the general public facts in relation to the conduct of the school system and its future plans that will enable it to judge of the general efficiency of the system and as to whether the community is receiving just returns for its expenditures.

The school report should be attractive in form. To secure this special attention should be made to arrangement, paragraphing, correct heading in paragraphs, illustrations, diagrams and index.

The modern school report should contain adequate financial statements of the receipts and expenditures of the school funds; discussion of the various departments into which the school system may be divided in reference to their progress, present state of efficiency and future development; such statistical tables as will present all the important facts relative to the financial and observation-disclosures of the system; such additional information in relation to the school system as may be of general public interest or which ought to be preserved for future reference.

What may be omitted from a school report depends largely upon the community in which the school report is issued. From the general viewpoint the following might be classified as not of general interest although some communities insist upon their inclusion in their reports. To the officers and members of all


affiliated unions of the Colorado


State Federation of Labor, greet:


You are hereby notified that the
eighteenth annual convention of the
Colorado State Federation of Labor
will convene at Trinidad, Colorado,
Tuesday, August 11, 1913, at 10
o'clock, for the purpose of conducting
say and all business that may properly
come before us.


Representation shall be as follows:


Sec. 1.—Each organization which
has been affiliated with the Federa-
tion, and in good standing at the
date of holding the convention, shall
be entitled to one delegate, and one
additional delegate for every 100
members or majority fraction
thereof; provided, no delegate
from any organization shall be al-
lowed to cast more than three votes.


Sec. 2.—Each craft body shall
be entitled to three delegates.


Sec. 3.—Delegates shall receive
their credentials from their local un-
ions in duplicate and send one copy
to the state federation secretary, two
weeks previous to the date of the
convention, and deliver the other to
the secretary of credentials. No
credentials shall be considered valid
unless more than two names of dele-
gates and alternates.


Sec. 4.—No proxies shall be al-
lowed under any circumstances, nor
shall any delegate be permitted to
vote in the name of any union, except
in so far as he or she is duly cred-
ited.

cessful one for the federation and all
organized labor of the state. From a
legislative standpoint, more meas-
ures affecting the interests of organ-
ized labor have been enacted late
than at any time in the history
of our organization.


Much good has been accumulated,
but there is still much to be done,
and at the coming convention there
will be need for the deliberation,
advice and consultation together of the
representatives of organized labor.


Several important changes to the
bylaws and constitution of the Fed-
eration are to be recommended.
We should at this convention form
a plan for statewide campaign of organisa-
tion.

annual convention, will be the most
important convention ever held by
the federation, we urge upon all affil-
iated organizations the advisability
and necessity of being represent-
ed by their full quota of delegates;
for you are all interested in the or-
ganization and should take part in
managing its affairs and shaping its
future course.

STRENGTHENING your craft organiza-
tion during his stay in Trinidad.


COLORADO STATE FEDERATION

tor car drivers race with our engines
for miles and when we think they are
going to slow up they dart across the
track right in the face of danger. All

are driving an engine you do not un-
derstand how it feels to see car slip
across the road few feet in front of
the engine."

handle division of the Santa Fe. It is
all too common along railroad lines in
this section of the country where high-
ways run parallel to railway tracks for
longer or shorter distances, only to
cross them eventually. Neither is it
one that should be suppressed by rail-
road officials alone for the proper pro-
tection of their engineers. Public au-
thority should take hand in the
premises.


An automobile driver who is so careless
of his own life that he will race with
a train for a crossing, can be set down
as having not the slightest regard for
the lives or the rights of others who
use the public roads. He is a menace
to society and should be treated as
such. Severe punishment should be
meted out to him. Indeed, it might be
well to corral such gentry and inquire
into their sanity. They must be mad.
They should be handled accordingly
and placed in restraint in institutions
where they cannot harm themselves
nor have a chance to harm others.


Undoubtedly, if conspicuous exam-
ples were made of some of these speed
omaniacs, the effect would be most sal-
utary. Others might thereby be cured
of their inclinations to indulge in such
folly.

passed by the recent session of Congress, the Interstate Commerce Commission will have in charge the work of ascertaining just what the entire railway system of the United States cost and its present value.

When it is realized that there are over 100,000 miles of main line to be inventoried, the data in regard to cost and value of 2,250,000 freight cars, 500,000 locomotives, together with shops, right-of-way, terminal properties, bridges, buildings, road equipment, general office equipment, and in fact every item owned or used by each and every railway, says the Railway Record, some little appreciation of the magnitude of this undertaking will be had.

The law calls for ascertaining "original cost to date with prices paid for property, materials, labor and services," the Commission to decide whether these disbursements have been legitimate and in the event they are found excessive to state what would have been proper figures at the time they were made.

A second requirement will be to ascertain the valuation in dollars of the cost of existing railway properties, in including real estate and equipment at present prices.

The third requirement is for the Commission to ascertain the historical cost of the railways as they stand today. In some cases it will be a physical impossibility to arrive at the figures, the records having been lost or destroyed intentionally or otherwise.

Fourth, the law calls for the ascertaining of the intangible values which might be included as an asset by the railway corporations. This would include franchises, good will, geographical location, etc., and must of necessity be largely a matter of personal opinion, there being no basis on which actual figures could be arrived at.

If no protest is made against these figures within thirty days, the valuation becomes final, but if any party to the proceedings does protest, the Commission is required to hold a hearing and to accept evidence tending to show that the figures named are incorrect after which the Commission is to make its final decision. During the progress of the investigation reports are to be made to Congress at the opening of each regular session.

It is expected that this work will employ the services of a large number of employees for the next five years. The estimated cost of the government was from $1,500,000 to $5,000,000. The expense of the inquiry to the railway companies will be fully as great, as it will involve them in an endless amount of clerical work, time and expense of officials, etc. It is quite reasonable to suppose that the railways will expend from $5,000,000 to $15,000,000 before the valuations are settled, and it will then be a question as to what value the figures have.

Mr. Calvin went over the situation Friday afternoon with James Mentally, retiring custodian, and was prepared to take up his old job Thursday.

St. Paul lost one of its oldest settlers Monday when William O. Davern died at the Davern homestead near Davern and West St. Paul, as a result of a second stroke of paralysis. Mr. Davern was 85 years old. Death occurred at R.J. while he was in a comatose state. Mr. Davern came to America in 1876 from County Clare, Ireland, and stopped for a time at Springfield, Mass. In 1885 he came to St. Paul and a few years later married Anne Maroney, also from County Clare, at that time a resident of St. Paul. She died in 1887 and their only child died a year later. Several years afterward Mr. Davern married Catherine Ryan of St. Paul, and they recently celebrated their fiftieth wedding anniversary. All of the thirteen children of the second marriage are living, with the exception of three. The other children are William A., Edward T., Joseph R., John, Nellie, Mrs. John Hail, Mr. Charles Sattler of St. Paul, James of Great Falls, Mont., and Benjamin Davern of Duluth. Mr. Davern was a member of territorial and state legislatures. To his efforts the setting aside of the military reservation on which Fort Snelling now stands was largely due.

After his service in the legislature, Mr. Davern was town supervisor and later school inspector and commissioner. The funeral took place from the above residence, Wednesday. Services were held at St. James Church. Interment was at Calvary cemetery.

Mrs. Nellie (née Conroy) aged 80 years, wife of Joseph Fried, died Saturday. The funeral took place from the undertaking rooms of Connolly and McDevitt Monday. Services were held at St. Joseph's Church at 2 p.m. Interment at Calvary cemetery.

The will of John Hart, formerly of Hart & Murphy, cigar manufacturers, was admitted to probate Wednesday by Judge H. W. Basils. The executors under the will are W. R. Barrett, Minneapolis, and Dennis A. Murphy, St. Paul. The estate is valued at $15,900. Two thirds of the property is left to Mrs. Hart for her life and the remaining to Miss Catherine Hart. After the death of Mrs. Hart, half the estate will go to Miss Hart, and the remaining half to be divided between the two daughters, Mrs. Alice Barrett, Minneapolis, and Mrs. Florence D. Donovan, Minneapolis.

On Thursday, June 25th, George G. Bond, aged 10 years, died at the home of his uncle, Edward Moriaxty, 255 Prescott St. The funeral took place Saturday from the above residence. Services were held at St. Michael's Church. Interment at Calvary cemetery.

The funeral of Frank S. Schubert, 80 years old, who died at the home of his sister, Miss Emma Schubert, 335 Carroll Ave., was held Friday from St. Joseph's Church. Interment was at Calvary cemetery. Death followed a long illness, which an operation six months ago failed to alleviate. Mr. Schubert lived in St. Paul Park for twenty-three years.

mer a partition has been erected
across the hall on the second floor,
giving considerable more space to
these offices.


Another much needed improvement
has been made in the armory where
two large 36-inch ventilators have been
installed which will greatly aid in the
dissemination of good air through the
building. In addition to this work, a
large heater has been installed in the
same building for the athletic de-
partment. Hot water will now be on
tap at any time during the training
season for the benefit of the athletes
who will need the use of hot showers
and baths.


A 1880 vault two stories in height
is to be added to the main building
and a machine shed 26x154 feet is
being built for the agricultural de-
partment.


The heating plant throughout the
college has been enlarged to a great
extent, 50 feet of 6-inch heating main
being added; 50 feet of 4-inch piping
and 25 feet of 2-inch high pressure
steam main for the new dairy build-
ing.


In order to make the seven deer
owned by the college, comfortable for
the winter a new and cosy deer house
has been constructed for their benefit
and several devices added to it for
their safety during the cold weather.
Cement flooring will take the place
of the old wooden in the cow barn,
and new floor to cover the west wing
of the barn, a space of 36x50 feet.


With these new extensive improve-
ments and additions to the college,
the working force has been kept very
busy during the summer but
it states that all the work should
be completed in another week or so
by the time that the college opens, Sept.
10. On the return of the students,
they will be greeted with a change in
the equipment of the college which
should be very pleasing, $35,600 worth
of improvements meaning added ad-
vantages for every student.


In fact, the agricultural college has
not looked so prosperous and pro-
ductive as it does today, standing in
the midst of a beautiful campus with
its clusters of beautiful buildings, its
handsome trees and a new with a
spirit of study pervading the atmos-
phere. New students will appreciate
its advantages and the older ones will
return with renewed loyalty to the
college which has done so much for
their betterment.
